newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Medeva looks to long-term value.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Medeva looks to long-term value.

text.p: Pharmaceuticals group Medeva Plc said on Wednesday investors should look at the long-term value being built for the company rather than concentrating on short-term problems.
As its share price slumped despite a 35 percent rise in interim profits, chief executive Bill Bogie told Reuters "people should see we are following our strategy."
"If people want to look at the short term that might colour their perceptions, but I am doing the best for the long term and building shareholder value," Bogie said.

The chief executive said news of a bladder cancer drug licensing agreement, the 4 million stg acquisition of a Belgian marketing company and a European distribution accord for its anaesthetic gases were all examples of Medeva's strategy to construct an international drug company in operation.

The short-term problems worrying the market on Wednesday were a drop in sales on appetite suppressant Ionamin following health scares in the U.S, and continued concerns about the emergence of other generic competitors in the U.S. market for attention deficit disorder drugs.
Bogie said sales of Ionamin had dropped to seven million stg in the first half of the year from 22 million in the second half of 1996.
Although he did not anticipate a speedy resolution, Bogie said "in the long-term we believe Ionamin has a good place in the market."

Bogie said sales of the group's main money-spinner, attention deficit drug Methylphenidate, advanced only six percent to 54 million stg due to changes in the way the drug was distributed. However, he said underlying sales were up by 16 percent.
"We have got to expect competition, but we are trying to move people on from looking at that," said Bogie.

Two further competitors for the tightly-controlled drug have been approved by U.S. authorities, but neither has started selling the product. Medeva accounted for 72 percent of the U.S. market in the first six months of 1997.
Medeva said the rise of sterling had reduced interim pre-tax profits by three million pounds, and the group expects a similarly adverse impact going forward.
Bogie told Reuters the acquisition of a small Belgian marketing company announced on Wednesday would open the door to the Benelux countries.
He said an acquisition to build marketing strength in German was a high priority, particularly as the company prepares to launch its range of asthma inhalers across Europe.
"We need to be there when the dry powder inhalers come through," said Bogie, adding "we are talking about 1999."
Bogie said Medeva was assessing a "a good flow" of late-stage products for licensing deals similar to that for Anthra Pharmaceuticals Inc's bladder cancer product announced earlier Wednesday.

Although the price for the product, which has still to be submitted for regulatory approval, had not been fixed, Bogie said comparable drugs cost around $800 a dose, and treatments required around half a dozen doses.

Medeva is also optimistic that a European distribution accord with Germany's Fresenius AG will ensure sustained profitability for its anaesthetic gases businesses, whose U.S. performance caused some disappointment.
Bogie said European sales would ensure the business, which was already profitable, was operating at full capacity, boosting long-term earnings growth.
